h: Follies, playgrounds and Grantham's famous names
p: Look out for the Orangery in the formal gardens, designed by Jeffry Wyatville in the early 1800s, which is a lovely spot on a sunny day. Out in the park, the Bellmount Tower is the folly you'll spot from a distance, perched at the end of a long avenue. It's a cracking walk to get there and a great backdrop for photos.

Families will want to know about the adventure playground, a big favourite with kids that can easily swallow an hour or more. With that, the gardens and the house, Belton works brilliantly as a full day out, and there's plenty of space for a picnic. Deer roam the parkland, so keep an eye out and keep your distance.

Pop into the church of St Peter and St Paul, right next to the house, too. It's full of monuments to generations of the Brownlow family and gives you a sense of just how long they were part of this place.
Allow at least half a day. The house and estate keep different arrangements through the year, so check what's open before you set off.

Grantham itself has a few famous names. Sir Isaac Newton went to school in the town, and his birthplace, Woolsthorpe Manor, is a short drive south and also cared for by the National Trust. The apple tree in the orchard there is famously linked to his thinking about gravity. Margaret Thatcher was born in Grantham too, and the town museum covers its history. Belvoir Castle, the grand home of the Dukes of Rutland, is a short drive west if you fancy another stately day.
